newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania to press on with NATO bid-Constantinescu.
newsitem.headline: Romania to press on with NATO bid-Constantinescu.

text.p: Romania's reformist president on Thursday vowed to doggedly pursue efforts to secure quick NATO membership for his country, despite U.S. resistance and the economic gap separating it from more advanced East Europeans.

"Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic deserve their place as front-runners for first-wave admission," Emil Constantinescu told a news conference marking his first 200 days in power since he ousted an ex-Communist in last year's polls.

"Romania's economic gap is offset by strategic and military arguments which make Romania very attractive for NATO," said Constantinescu, who will meet Chancellor Helmuth Kohl in Bonn next week seeking to sway German support behind Romania's bid.
Constantinescu expressed no hard feelings over Washington's choice, announced two weeks ago, to support membership only for the three favourites, passing over Romania and Slovenia.

"It is both President Clinton's decision and my decision that we...should build a strategic partnership between Romania and the United States. This partnership with the United States is not contingent on the outcome of the Madrid (summit).
Romanian and Slovenian leaders say their countries' admission would strengthen NATO's southern flank.

Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea, who returned from a visit to Washington on Wednesday, delivered an invitation for Clinton to visit Romania after the July 8-9 summit in Madrid, where the alliance is due to announce its first eastward expansion.
The White House has yet to respond to the invitation. A Clinton visit would be the first to Romania by a U.S. president to Romania since the 1989 fall of communism.
Constantinescu said Romania had come a long way since he and a centrist govenment took power last November. But much had to be done to put the economy on a solid market footing.
"Before the November elections, we stood no chance of being considered as likely candidates for NATO membership," he said.

"Now Slovakia, once cited alongside the Czech Republic as a likely candidate, has vanished not only from first-wave, but also from second-wave candidates, due to the ultra-nationalist tendencies of its government.
"This should serve as a warning for us too."
Western leaders have praised the inclusion of ethnic Hungarians in Romania's government and new treaties with Hungary and Ukraine ending rifts over borders and minorities.

Constantinescu hailed the pact signed this month with Ukraine, ratified by the lower house of parliament on Thursday, as a big step towards building regional security. It must still clear the Senate, where centrists also have a majority.
He praised French President Jacques Chirac's support for Romania and Slovenia, repeated during last weekend's Group of Seven summit in Denver.
"Jacques Chirac and leaders of other important states, including Canada, have shown they consider this matter (Romania's NATO bid) as one of their own problems," said Constantinescu.
"Now it is up to us to consolidate the reforms, it is up to the way in which Romanians react to challenges posed by the reforms and the way in which the economy reacts."

Constantinescu travels on Friday to the Netherlands, current European Union president, for a gathering intended to brief Central and East European leaders about EU enlargement prospects after the EU summit in Amsterdam last week.
